column21:
🧭 Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis; full relevant Core coverage and the fused RadPrimer/STATdx article were reviewed.
📖 Summary
  • A hemorrhagic ovarian cyst is hemorrhage into a functional ovarian cyst, most commonly a corpus luteum cyst; bleeding may also occur in a follicular cyst.
  • The core diagnostic task is to prove ovarian origin, recognize avascular blood products, and identify rupture, active hemorrhage, or torsion.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings

Ultrasound
  • Endovaginal ultrasound with color Doppler is the best primary imaging test.
  • Classic internal patterns include diffuse echogenicity, fine reticular or lace-like fibrin strands, retracting clot, and a fluid-fluid or debris level.
  • Posterior acoustic enhancement or through transmission supports cystic behavior even when blood products make the lesion appear solid.
  • Clot and fibrin should have no internal Doppler flow; peripheral ovarian parenchymal or corpus luteum flow may be prominent.
  • Core emphasizes retractile clot with concave margins and absent Doppler flow versus a true solid mural nodule with a convex margin and internal flow.
CT
  • CT may show an adnexal cyst with high-attenuation blood products, fluid-fluid level, peripheral enhancement, and hemoperitoneum.
  • Rupture clues include a sentinel clot near the ovary, a cyst-wall defect, and active adnexal bleeding.
MR Imaging
  • Blood-product signal is variable with blood age, hematocrit, protein concentration, hemoglobin form, and clot formation or retraction.
  • T1 fat-suppressed imaging is useful because persistent high signal after fat suppression supports blood rather than macroscopic fat; internal clot should not enhance.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Endometrioma: homogeneous low-level echoes, often T1 hyperintense with T2 shading, and persistence rather than short-interval resolution.
  • Dermoid: echogenic or shadowing components, Rokitansky nodule, calcification, or fat; fat-containing components suppress on fat-saturated MRI.
  • Ovarian neoplasm: papillary projections, mural nodules, thick or irregular septa/walls, solid enhancing components, or internal vascularity.
  • Ectopic pregnancy: the ring-of-fire sign is nonspecific; a corpus luteum is intraovarian, whereas a tubal ectopic is typically extraovarian and may move separately with probe pressure.
  • Torsion may coexist; preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because of dual ovarian blood supply and possible intermittent torsion.
📌 Clinical / Management Pivots
  • In reproductive-age patients, a classic hemorrhagic cyst measuring 5 cm or less needs no follow-up; larger than 5 cm receives short-interval ultrasound follow-up in about 6-12 weeks.
  • Most hemorrhagic cysts resolve or substantially decrease within about 6-8 weeks; persistence raises consideration of endometrioma or another structural lesion.
  • Early postmenopausal hemorrhagic-appearing cysts require follow-up for resolution; late postmenopausal lesions should not be assumed physiologic and should prompt concern for malignancy and consideration of surgical evaluation.
  • Stable rupture is usually managed supportively; hemodynamic instability, significant intraperitoneal hemorrhage, torsion, or severe persistent symptoms may require surgery.
⭐ Super Summary
  • Think ovarian + cystic + avascular internal blood products + expected interval resolution; escalate when there is enhancing/vascular solid tissue, torsion, or major active hemorrhage.

column11: Why can a hemorrhagic ovarian cyst evolve from an echogenic or solid-appearing lesion into a web-like or retracting-clot pattern on ultrasound?
column12: Hemorrhage enters a functional ovarian cyst, most often a corpus luteum. The source describes a changing mixture of liquid blood, fibrin, and clot: acutely, blood can make the cyst diffusely echogenic and mimic solid tissue; as clot organizes and retracts and the clot dissolves, fibrin strands and retracting clot create the characteristic web-like/reticular or geometric intracystic interfaces. Because these internal structures are blood products rather than perfused tissue, they remain avascular on Doppler. The cystic fluid background can still produce posterior acoustic enhancement, preserving the clue that the lesion is fundamentally cystic.

column11: Why does preserved ovarian Doppler flow not exclude adnexal torsion?
column12: The ovary has dual arterial inflow: the ovarian artery supplies it laterally and a uterine-artery branch supplies it medially. Twisting of the vascular pedicle may therefore leave detectable flow through one vascular route, and intermittent torsion-detorsion can also restore transient flow. Imaging interpretation must therefore integrate ovarian enlargement, edema/inhomogeneity, peripheral follicles, abnormal position, free fluid, and—when present—the highly specific twisted vascular pedicle rather than using preserved flow as an exclusion criterion.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings

Ultrasound
  • Endovaginal ultrasound with color Doppler is the best primary imaging test.
  • Classic internal patterns include diffuse echogenicity, fine reticular or lace-like fibrin strands, retracting clot, and a fluid-fluid or debris level.
  • Posterior acoustic enhancement or through transmission supports cystic behavior even when blood products make the lesion appear solid.
  • Clot and fibrin should have no internal Doppler flow; peripheral ovarian parenchymal or corpus luteum flow may be prominent.

  • CT may show an adnexal cyst with high-attenuation blood products, fluid-fluid level, peripheral enhancement, and hemoperitoneum.
  • Rupture clues include a sentinel clot near the ovary, a cyst-wall defect, and active adnexal bleeding.

  • Blood-product signal is variable with blood age, hematocrit, protein concentration, hemoglobin form, and clot formation or retraction.
